title: Structural equation modelling
text:
In this practical, we will use tools from the lavaan package to fit a structural equation model. We will first look at how to construct latent variables using confirmatory factor analysis, and then use these latent variables to predict performance on another measure.
Structural equation modelling is a particularly popular technique in developmental psychology, allowing researchers to test how particular traits or abilities measured early in development can predict subsequent outcomes. For today’s practical, we will analyse data collected in the Numerical Cognition Lab led by Professor Silke Goebel. The project looked at whether children’s numeric and cognitive skills measured in Year 1 predicted mathematical performance in Year 3.
The team have shared their data openly on the Open Science Framework (we’ll talk more about this in Lecture 11). We will be loading and working with a subset of the available data today, which have been relabelled to make their relationship to one another transparent for the practical.






Learning objectives



As a reminder, this week’s learning objectives are to:

Differentiate between univariate and multivariate analytical approaches
Describe the measurement and structural components of SEM
Outline the five key stages involved in conducting SEM
Understand how to read a path model
Discuss factors that affect the implementation and generalisability of SEM

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
2.1 Create a script
Start with the usual set-up steps for the practical sessions:

Open your ARM_Practicals.Rproj file in RStudio
Create a new script and save it in your scripts/ folder as ARM7_SEM.R
Download the data for the Week 7 practical from the VLE, and save it in your data/ folder.







Tip



If you don’t have this folder on your current machine, repeat the set-up steps outlined in 0_SetUp.pdf from Week 1.

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
2.2 Load packages
We will be using two packages today, lavaan and semPlot. Install them in the usual way, using install.packages() or the Packages tab.
Once they are installed, add the following lines at the top of your script to load them ready for today.

# Load packages
library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
2.3 Load data
Once you have downloaded and saved the data from the VLE, you can load it into R as follows:

# Load data
maths_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM7_data_maths.csv")

Inspect the maths_dat dataset you have now loaded. You’ll notice that there are many more variables compared to previous weeks—18 to be precise, yet this is only a subset of the available data! Variables labelled with t1 correspond to measures administered when the children were in Year 1; variables labelled with t3 correspond to measures administered when the children were in Year 3. You should see the following variables:

id: a unique identifier for each participant
t1_age_m: age in months at T1
t1_tc*: variables corresponding to the transcoding of numbers at T1, including writing, identification, and reading
t1_nc*: variables corresponding to number comparison tasks at T1, including symbolic (numbers) and non-symbolic (dot) comparisons, with comparisons that were closer and further apart.
t3_mr: mathematical reasoning ability at T3
The final six columns reflect additional speeded arithmetic measures at T3. These are only relevant for the “Challenge yourself” task at the end.

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
3.1 One-factor solution

3.1.1 Model specification
Our first step to constructing the measurement model is model specification. In the simplest case here, we have one latent variable which predicts performance on all nine measures.
We can specify this as follows:

# Specify model formula
numerical_1f <- "numerical =~ t1_tc1 + t1_tc2 + t1_tc3 + 
                              t1_nc1 + t1_nc2 + t1_nc3 + 
                              t1_nc4 + t1_nc5 + t1_nc6"







Keyboard shortcuts



Note that the usual Ctrl+Enter keyboard shortcut does not work so well for these model formulas. You will either need to (1) repeat the shortcut as it progresses through each line of code; (2) highlight the whole chunk before using the keyboard shortcut; or (3) highlight the whole chunk and click run.


We give our latent variable a name, numerical, and specify that it is measured by (=~) the nine variables that we have listed by name (separated by the + operator). We’ve stored this formula as an object in R, called numerical_1f, ready to use in model fitting.
The model we are fitting therefore looks like this:





Path diagram depicting all 9 numerical measures as a single latent construct.






3.1.2 Model identification
We won’t worry too much about model identification here—we would get an error message if this was a problem! But just so that you have a worked example and you can interpret the model information below, we can see that the model is (over-)identified as follows:

Number of data points: N = (p*(p+1))/2), where p is the number of measured variables. We have 9 measured variables (3 transcoding tasks, 6 number comparison tasks), so this can be expanded as follows:

N = (9*(9+1))/2 = 45

Number of parameters: you can see in the diagram that the first loading is fixed to 1 by default (the marker method described in the lecture), as represented by the dashed line. We count the remaining free parameters to be estimated, including the remaining factor loadings (8), variance of latent variables (1), and error variance for each measured variable (9) = 18 free parameters to be estimated
Degrees of freedom: Number of data points (45) - Number of parameters (18) = 27.

The model is over-identified (= good).




3.1.3 Model estimation and evaluation
Now we’ve specified our model and checked its suitability, the next step is model estimation. Let’s fit it to the data!

# Fit model
fit_1f <- cfa(numerical_1f, data = maths_dat)

# Print output including fit indices
summary(fit_1f, fit.measures = TRUE)

We use the cfa() function here as we are only testing the relationship between the latent variable(s) and measured variables, via a confirmatory factor analysis.
The first section of the model output tells us about the model fitting process, including the number of iterations needed to fit the model alongside the estimator and optimization method used. You can also see the number of observations included (you should see that this matches the number of rows in your dataset) alongside the number of model parameters and degrees of freedom as we counted up above.
We specified that we wanted measures of model fit to be included in our output, and so the next section shows a number of fit indices—including CFI, TLI, and RMSEA as we discussed in the lecture. Based on your notes, do you think this model is a good fit?

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
3.2 Two-factor solution
Before we delve into exploratory model modification steps, we can already consider an alternative model based on theory. In this case, the researchers expected that transcoding and number comparison reflect separate skills, and we could see this in the task correlations.
Let’s specify and fit a two-factor solution based on this theory. We can estimate the transcoding latent variable from the three measures of transcoding (t1_tc*), and num_comparison latent variable from the remaining six tasks (t1_nc*). We won’t check model identification manually this time, but we will be able to see this information in the output.

# Specify 2-factor model 
numerical_2f <- "transcoding =~ t1_tc1 + t1_tc2 + t1_tc3 
                 num_comparison =~ t1_nc1 + t1_nc2 + t1_nc3 + 
                                   t1_nc4 + t1_nc5 + t1_nc6"

# Fit model 
fit_2f <- cfa(numerical_2f, data = maths_dat)

# Inspect output, including fit indices
summary(fit_2f, fit.measures = TRUE)

What do you think of the new model fit?
The bottom section of the output specifies the parameter estimates for the model. It can be easier to interpret these on a plot, which you can create using the following line of code:

# Plot model
semPaths(fit_2f, whatLabels = "std")

We’ve specified that the parameter estimates are presented in standardised format so that we can compare the estimates across different variables. You can change the whatLabels argument to “par” if you want them to be in the original units of the variables (as presented in the CFA output by default).

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
3.3 Model modification
The above 2-factor model looks to be a pretty good fit. For the sake of this practical, let’s consider whether there’s any other parameters we could add to make it even better.
The standardised parameters indicate that the factor loadings are all sensible, and so we should keep all the tasks in the model. But what about extra parameters? We can ask lavaan to show us the change in chi-square statistic when different possible parameters are added. We specify sort = true so that it shows us the biggest improvements at the top of the list:

# Modification indices 
modindices(fit_2f, sort = TRUE)

The output tells us that the largest change (mi) would come from adding a covariance (~~) between the variables t1_nc1 and t1_nc6. You can try adding this to your model formula, and inspect the resulting model fit:

# Specify new model formula with covariance
numerical_2f_m <- "transcoding =~ t1_tc1 + t1_tc2 + t1_tc3 
                   num_comparison =~ t1_nc1 + t1_nc2 + t1_nc3 + 
                                     t1_nc4 + t1_nc5 + t1_nc6
                   t1_nc1 ~~ t1_nc6"

# Fit model 
fit_2f_m <- cfa(numerical_2f_m, data = maths_dat)

# Inspect output, including fit indices
summary(fit_2f_m, fit.measures = TRUE)

However, we would only want to proceed with adding model parameters if they make theoretical sense: there might not be an intuitive explanation for the errors to be correlated in these two tasks beyond other tasks. Indeed, the model fit was already very good without this additional parameter, and adding more parameters risks overfitting (i.e., the model would become less able to generalise to new datasets). In this case, the simpler 2-factor model is preferred.

title: Structural equation modelling
section: 4.1 Predicting mathematical reasoning from early numeric skills
text:
4.1 Predicting mathematical reasoning from early numeric skills
In our new model formula, we should specify how our latent constructs are measured just as we did before. However, we can now add a structural part to test whether mathematical reasoning (t3_mr) is predicted by (~) our two latent variables. This part of the model formula should feel familiar—we’ve been writing model formulas in similar ways in earlier practicals.
Specify the model, and use the sem() function this time to fit it.

# Longitudinal model specification
pred_mr <- "   # measurement model 
               transcoding =~ t1_tc1 + t1_tc2 + t1_tc3
               num_comparison =~ t1_nc1 + t1_nc2 + t1_nc3 + 
                                 t1_nc4 + t1_nc5 + t1_nc6
                              
               # regressions
               t3_mr ~ transcoding + num_comparison"

# Fit model
fit_predict <- sem(pred_mr, data = maths_dat)

Inspect the model fit as before, and plot the path diagram.
Is the model a good fit to the data? Which early skills are the stronger predictor of mathematical reasoning performance?

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
4.2 Dealing with missing data
Take a look at your SEM model output. What do you notice about the number of observations used in the model, relative to when we fitted the measurement model using only Year 1 data?
In the lecture, we mentioned some possible ways of dealing with missing data, including using a different fitting algorithm called Full Information Maximum Likelihood. While these techniques require several assumptions about the nature of missingness in the dataset, the actual implementation using lavaan is surprisingly simple: we just need to add an argument within the sem() to specify that we want missingness to be addressed using (full information) maximum likelihood estimation. Try adding missing = "ML" to your SEM model above, and inspect the results.

title: Structural equation modelling
text:
5.1 Challenge yourself
Mathematical reasoning is only one aspect of mathematical ability in developing learners. The researchers were also interested in speeded arithmetic skills, which they measured in Year 3 using 6 different tasks (labelled t3_add1, t3_add2, t3_sub1, t3_sub2, t3_mult, t3_div).
Fit a new model in which your early numeric skills (transcoding, number comparison) predict subsequent performance in speeded arithmetic, captured by a third latent variable (as depicted below). You will need to specify how this latent variable is measured, and then use it in a regression path.





Simplified path diagram showing how number comparison and transcoding skills measured in Year 1 predict speeded arithmetic skills in Year 3.

title: Stochastic methods
text:
This practical will introduce the concept of bootstrapping for both descriptive and inferential statistics. Along the way, we will learn about a very useful feature in programming languages: loops! These allow us to repeat tasks multiple times, and increase the efficiency of our work.
For the first part of this practical, we will simulate some data. This is a useful thing to be able to do as it allows us to compare our bootstrapped results to the “true mean” we used to generate our data. In the second part, we will use a real dataset from a study of wellbeing in pregnancy. We’ll introduce that later on!






Learning objectives



As a reminder, this week’s learning objectives are to:

Explain the role and utility of stochastic methods in statistical analysis
Outline the logic and procedure of bootstrapping
Describe how the non-parametric bootstrap avoids distributional assumptions
Apply bootstrap techniques to estimate a range of statistical parameters
Relate these core principles to a variety of statistical tasks

title: Stochastic methods
text:
2.1 For loops
A for loop increments a variable each time around the loop, for a set number of repetitions. Here is the simplest possible for loop—what do you think it does?

# Example "for" loop
for (i in 1:10) {
  print(i)
}

Add this code to your script and execute it. You should get a list of the numbers 1 to 10 in the console. What’s happening here is that we’re telling the computer to increment the variable i, starting at 1 and continuing to a value of 10. Each time round the loop, the commands inside the {curly brackets} are repeated. In this case, we’re just printing the value of i to the console.
We can scale this up to do more complex things. For example, we could generate some random numbers and put their mean into a list. To do this, we first need to create a vector to store the output. Then, through each iteration of the loop, we calculate the mean of 20 randomly generated numbers and store it in the i-th entry of the vector.

# Create an empty vector to store output
mean_list <- NULL

# In each of 10 runs through the loop
for (i in 1:10){
  
  # Generate 20 random numbers from a normal distribution
  random_n <- rnorm(20)
  
  # Calculate the mean
  mean_val <- mean(random_n)
  
  # Store the mean value in the corresponding (i) vector entry
  mean_list[i] <- mean_val
}

# Print the output
mean_list

Run this section of code: you should see it outputs a list of means, and that you now have this list of means stored in your R environment. This simple process can be very useful for bootstrapping and other stochastic methods.






Coding tip!



Note that we wrote each step out in full in the above loop to illustrate each step in turn. However, the programming whizzes amongst you might spot that we could have written the contents of the loop much more concisely. We could nest the data generation function inside the mean function and assigning it directly to the output vector: mean_list[i] <- mean(rnorm(20)). Brackets are interpreted from the inside out, so the rnorm() data generation is completed before the mean() is computed on it.
Either option is fine: coding concisely versus in clear readable steps can each be better in different situations.

title: Stochastic methods
text:
2.2 While loops
An alternative then is the while loop. Instead of running for a fixed number of times, the loop terminates only when a certain condition is met. Here is a very simple example:

# Start with i = 0
i <- 0              

# Example "while" loop
while (i < 10){     # providing i is less than 10
  i <- i + 1        # increase i by 1
  print(i)          # print new value of i
}

This does exactly the same as the first for loop example: it repeats ten times, increasing the value of i each time and printing it out. Although it takes more lines of code, it can be used in interesting ways.
Try modifying the code above so that instead of increasing by a fixed value, it adds a random number generated from a normal distribution. The rnorm() function will help you do this. How many times do we go round the loop when the mean of the normal distribution is 0, versus when it is 0.5?


Show the code
# Modified version 1: Mean = 0

i <- 0              # start with i = 0

while (i < 10){                 # providing i is less than 10
  i <- i + rnorm(1, mean = 0)   # increase i by random number
  print(i)                      # print new value of i
}

# Modified version 1: Mean = 0.5

i <- 0              # reset start to i = 0

while (i < 10){                   # providing i is less than 10
  i <- i + rnorm(1, mean = 0.5)   # increase i by random number
  print(i)                         # print new value of i
}

title: Stochastic methods
text:
3.1 Generate skewed data
First, let’s create some simulated data to work with. This is useful for understanding how things work as we can control the properties of the data ourselves1. In this case, we’ll make sure that the data are not normally distributed by generating them from an exponential distribution.





Histogram of example simulated dataset




We can do this using the rexp() function. Find out how it works by typing help(rexp). Then create a variable, a, with 40 samples (n) from this distribution, leaving the default rate parameter as 1.
Plot a histogram of your simulated dataset using hist(a), and calculate the true mean. This will be slightly different to the person next to you, as you each generated a random sample from scratch.

title: Stochastic methods
text:
3.2 Run the bootstrapping
Now let’s resample the mean many times in a loop. Start by creating an empty variable to store the means in. Let’s call it all_means:

all_means <- NULL

Then create a for loop that will repeat 1000 times. Inside the loop, we need to do two things as follows:

# Resample with replacement from the synthetic data (a)
b <- sample(a, replace = TRUE)

# Calculate the mean of the resampled data, and store it in all_means
all_means[i] <- mean(b) 

Embed the two lines in your loop to achieve the resampling.
Create a histogram of the all_means vector using the hist() function. It should look like a normal distribution, despite the underlying data coming from a non-normal distribution. (Hint: if you get a single block only, make sure you’ve embedded your code in a loop!)
We can get R to work out the 95% confidence intervals using the quantile function:

ci <- quantile(all_means, c(0.025, 0.975))

Print the values of ci. These are the bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals of the mean.
Try running through the loop and this line several times (but with the same starting sample of data). What do you notice?

title: Stochastic methods
text:
4.1 Introducing the data
This week we will work with data from Dr Catherine Preston’s research group. Dr Lydia Munns (a former PhD student in the department) was interested in how bodily experiences during pregnancy are associated with wellbeing. They administered several questionnaires to >200 pregnant women, including body dissatisfaction and depression which we will look at today. If you’re interested in this topic, you can access the full paper here.
Download the data from the VLE page for this practical, and save it in your data/ folder as usual. Read it into R:

bumps_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM5_data_bumps.csv")

Inspect the dataset. You should see we have the following variables:

body_diss: body dissatisfaction, as measured by the Body Understanding Measure for Pregnancy Scale (BUMPs)
anxiety: anxiety, as measured by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale
depression: depression, as measured by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale

We will just use the depression scores today, but anxiety scores are retained in the dataset in case you later want to apply what you learn to a new example.

title: Stochastic methods
text:
4.2 Run a linear regression
The authors were interested in how body dissatisfaction during pregnancy predicted depression scores. Fit a simple linear model as follows, then call summary() on the fitted object to inspect the output.

# Fit a linear model
bumps_lm <- lm(depression ~ body_diss, data = bumps_dat)

The intercept and slope of the regression model are stored in the output variable, which you can access in a more direct way using bumps_lm$coefficients. You can select the slope for body dissatisfaction specifically using bumps_lm$coefficients["body_diss"]. Run this now and store the entry in your environment as true_slope, it should have the value ~0.09. This means that every unit increase in the body dissatisfaction scale is associated with a ~0.1 increase on the depression scale.
We can also use these extracted coefficients to plot a regression line on a scatterplot. Try running the following code, and inspecting the figure in the Plots window:

library(ggplot2)

# Create scatterplot 
ggplot(bumps_dat, aes(x = body_diss, y = depression)) + 
  theme_bw() +    # black and white theme
  geom_point() +  # data points 
  geom_abline(intercept = bumps_lm$coefficients["(Intercept)"], # model regression
              slope = bumps_lm$coefficients["body_diss"])

We loaded ggplot2 here as one of the most widely used data visualisation packages in R. It comes as part of the tidyverse set that we have loaded in other practicals. This code specifies the dataframe we want to use for plotting (bumps_lm), and the x and y variables we want to aesthetically map on the plot. With this as a foundation, we specify a black and white theme, add points to represent the raw data, then a line with the intercept and slope values taken from the fitted model object.

title: Stochastic methods
section: 4.3 Compute bootstrapped 95% CIs on the intercept and slope
text:
4.3 Compute bootstrapped 95% CIs on the intercept and slope
To do the bootstrapping, we need to sample the rows from the dataframe, so that the relationship between variables is preserved (i.e., the correct pairings between each participant’s scores). To do this, we create an index variable that contains the same number of entries as there are rows of the dataframe:

# Create data index for resampling
index <- 1:nrow(bumps_dat)

Now create a loop to perform 1000 bootstrap samples. Within each iteration, you will need to create a resample_index by resampling the index variable (just as we did when resampling values earlier).
You can then use the resampled variable you have created to extract the corresponding rows from the dataset as follows:

# Use resampled index to generate data based on row numbers
resample_dat <- bumps_dat[resample_index,]

On each iteration, repeat the regression with the sampled data and store the slope in a vector (as we did for bootstrapping means).
Once you have run the bootstrapping, use the quantile() function to calculate 95% confidence intervals. These should be approximately [0.07, 0.14].


Show the code
# Create data index for resampling
index <- 1:nrow(bumps_dat)

# Create vector to store slopes
all_slopes <- NULL

# For each of 1000 iterations
for (i in 1:1000){
  
  # Resample the row numbers
  resample_index <- sample(index, replace = TRUE)
  
  # Use the resample row numbers to select rows from the dataset
  resample_dat <- bumps_dat[resample_index,]
  
  # Run a new linear regression model on the resampled data
  new_mod <- lm(depression ~ body_diss, data = resample_dat)
  
  # Extract and store new slope value
  all_slopes[i] <- new_mod$coefficients["body_diss"]
  
}

# Calculate 95% confidence intervals from distribution of slopes
quantile(all_slopes, c(0.025, 0.975))


If you have time, see if you can add these new slopes to your figure. You might wish to change the linetype or colour of your new lines so that your confidence intervals are distinguished from your original slope. ggplot2 is a very flexible tool with lots of opportunities for customising your plots, so you can have fun trying to make your figure look more visually appealing by googling what you wish to change.


Show the code
# Extract and store CI values
lowerCI <- quantile(all_slopes, 0.025)
upperCI <- quantile(all_slopes, 0.975)

### Plot original regression line plus boostrapped 95% confidence intervals
ggplot(bumps_dat, aes(x = body_diss, y = depression)) + 
  theme_bw() +    # black and white theme
  geom_point() +  # data points
  
  # original regression line
  geom_abline(intercept = bumps_lm$coefficients[1], 
              slope = bumps_lm$coefficients[2], colour = "black") + 
  
  # lower confidence interval 
  geom_abline(intercept = bumps_lm$coefficients[1], 
              slope = lowerCI, colour = "blue") + 
  
  # upper confidence interval 
  geom_abline(intercept = bumps_lm$coefficients[1], 
              slope = upperCI, colour = "blue")


Show the code
## Note you could also extract and  use the bootstrapped intercepts in these to improve further

text:
5.1 Challenge yourself
In standard cases, we might prefer to take “shortcuts” and use pre-programmed functions in R. Try using Google to see what packages already exist for bootstrapping. Can you get them up and running using online resources?
Alternatively, you could repeat the steps today in analysing the anxiety variable, and expand the code to calculate the bootstrapped intercept and slope coefficient.

title: Mixed effects models
text:
In this practical, we will have a go at using a mixed effects model to analyse data from a factorial experiment.
Mixed effects models first became popular in psycholinguistics, where researchers want to generalise their findings beyond their specific sample of people and the specific words that they selected to include in their experiment. Nowadays, many areas of psychology use mixed effects models to analyse their data.
We will use a psycholinguistic dataset today, which I (Emma) collected together with Professors Lisa Henderson and Gareth Gaskell. We were interested in how children’s memory for new words changes over sleep. We taught children the names of unusual animals and plants, and tested their memory after 12 hours using a picture naming task. In one condition, this 12 hours was over the day and so participants spent the time awake. In the other condition, this 12 hours spanned the night and so participants spent the time asleep. We will use a subset of the data for demonstration purposes today, but you can read more about the study here if you are interested.






Learning objectives



As a reminder, this week’s learning objectives are to:

Describe some limitations of ANOVA and regression
Explain the benefits of modelling variation within and between groups
Define and distinguish between fixed and random effects
Interpret the key components and output of a basic mixed effects model
Evaluate the benefits and challenges associated with mixed effects modelling

title: Mixed effects models
text:
2.1 Create a script
Start with the usual set-up steps for the practical sessions:

Open your ARM_Practicals.Rproj file in RStudio
Create a new script and save it in your scripts/ folder as ARM3_mixed-effects.R
Download the data for the Week 3 practical from the VLE, and save it in your data/ folder.







Tip



If you don’t have this folder on your current machine, repeat the set-up steps outlined in the Set-up steps from Week 1.

title: Mixed effects models
text:
2.2 Load packages
We will need the following packages for today’s session, so add these lines of code at the top of your script. Run them so that they are ready to use. If you don’t have the packages already installed on your device, you will need to install them first using install.packages() as we have in previous weeks.

library(tidyverse)  # for data wrangling
library(lme4)       # for mixed effects models
library(lmerTest)   # for p-values

R defaults to scientific notation for very small numbers, which can be hard to interpret if you’re not used to them. You can add this line of code to switch it off:

options(scipen = 999)

title: Mixed effects models
text:
2.3 Load trial-level data
Now read in the data from your data/ folder.

sleep_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM3_data_sleep.csv")

The dataset consists of the following variables:

ppt_id: a unique identifier for each participant
sleep: whether participants had slept between learning and the test (no, yes)
novel_pic: whether the picture presented was a previously unseen picture (yes) or the same one used in training (no)
item: the word trained and tested
acc: whether the picture was correctly named (1) or not (0)
RT: the response time for correctly named pictures (ms)

Remember that you can click the grid icon in your enviroment window to see what your new dataset looks like. You should see that it includes one row per trial per participant. You might see that the RT column contains a lot of missing data (NA). This is because we were only interested in response time when the answer was correct (acc = 1).

title: Mixed effects models
text:
3.1 T-test of participant averages
We can’t run a t-test on the dataset as it is because it violates the assumption of independence: we have multiple responses from each participant. Instead, we need to create an average response time for each condition for each participant. You can copy and paste this code to achieve this:

ppt_means <- sleep_dat %>%      # take the existing data frame
  group_by(ppt_id, sleep) %>%   # for each value of ppt_id & sleep condition
  summarise(n_trials = sum(!is.na(RT)),  # count valid RT values
            mean_RT = mean(RT, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% # & calculate the mean RT
  pivot_wider(names_from = sleep, names_prefix = "sleep_", 
              values_from = c(n_trials, mean_RT)) # reformat into a wide data

There are some new data-wrangling functions here that you might find helpful for future reference. You don’t need to understand this in great detail for the purpose of this practical, but there’s an explainer in the note below if you’re interested.






Data wrangling with the tidyverse package





We have created a new object called ppt_means by taking our dataset, and then (%>%) grouping by participant ppt_id and sleep condition. Then (%>%) we feed this to the summarise() function to calculate some summary variables for each combination of those groups.
The first summary variable counts up how many RT values there are to average across (i.e., how many are !not missing data (is.na()) on this variable. We’ve called that new variable n_trials.
The second summary variable calculates the mean of the RT values. We’ve called it mean_RT, and specified that it should be calculated using the mean() function. We have had to tell it to remove the missing values when doing this (na.rm = TRUE).
Finally, the last line (pivot_wider()) rearranges the dataset into wide format, so that we have one participant per row. We’ve used the values of the sleep variable to name each new column, and specified that those columns should include both the number of trials and mean RT.
If you’re interested in learning how to clean and format your own data, the DataCamp course Introduction to the Tidyverseis highly recommended.



Inspect the new object that you have created. You should see that you now have just one row per participant. The first two columns tell us the number of trials used to calculate each participant’s average for each sleep condition, and then the last two columns tell us the mean RT for each condition.
What do you make of this? Is it right that we will treat each participant’s average score the same in the analysis, even though some are estimated from fewer trials than others?
Now use the t.test() function to run a paired t-test. Use the internet or the help files to help you. Your output should look as follows:



    Paired t-test

data:  ppt_means$mean_RT_sleep_no and ppt_means$mean_RT_sleep_yes
t = 4.5257, df = 30, p-value = 0.00008858
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 303.8399 803.5749
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       553.7074 








Hint!





You will need to use the $ to specify the column names, in the format dataframe$variable.





Show solution
# Code for paired t-test between two columns 
t.test(ppt_means$mean_RT_sleep_no, ppt_means$mean_RT_sleep_yes, paired = TRUE)

title: Mixed effects models
text:
3.2 T-test of word averages
The t-test on participant means tells us that that sleep effect likely generalises to other people in the population. What if we also want to know whether it generalises to other words that we might have chosen to teach?
If you have time, repeat the steps above but for items instead of participants: create a set of item means by calculating an average RT for each target and condition. Then run a paired t-test. Are the results consistent with the participant version? If you’ve already spent a while doing the above steps, move straight onto the next section.


Show solution
# Calculate item means 
item_means <- sleep_dat %>%     # take the existing data frame
  group_by(item, sleep) %>%     # for each id and condition
  summarise(n_trials = sum(!is.na(RT)),           # count valid trials
            mean_RT = mean(RT, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% # & calculate the mean RT 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sleep, names_prefix = "sleep_", 
              values_from = c(n_trials, mean_RT)) # reformat into wide format

# Run by-items t-test
t.test(item_means$mean_RT_sleep_no, item_means$mean_RT_sleep_yes, paired = TRUE)

title: Mixed effects models
text:
5.1 Exploring the random coefficients
Our model included random intercepts: that is, it modelled how each participant or item’s average response time deviated from the overall mean. We can find out more about this spread by plotting the random effects as follows:

dotplot.ranef.mer(ranef(mod1))







Tip!



You might want to increase the size of the plot window (bottom right quadrant), so that you can see the plots more clearly.


You can navigate between the two plots to see which participant IDs and words were fastest (-) and slowest (+) overall, relative to the overall intercept. We’re not typically interested in these values but the information comes for free in the modelling processes, and it can be a useful check to see if any of your experimental stimuli are behaving strangely.
If you want a little joy, enter the name of the fastest item into a Google image search to see why children enjoyed learning that word! :)

title: Mixed effects models
text:
5.2 Adding random slopes
Typically, we also want to consider adding random slopes to model variation in our fixed effects. Do some participants/words show larger sleep effects than others?
Let’s start by adding a random slope for the effect of sleep across different items. We do this by adding the predictor alongside the intercept in the random effects part of the formula:

mod2 <- lmer(RT ~ sleep + (1|ppt_id) + (1+sleep|item), data = sleep_dat) 

You should now see that the model lists a variance component for the effect of sleep on the item grouping, and the fixed effect coefficient has changed slightly.
Now create a third model (mod3) which also includes a random slope for the effect of sleep across different participants (ppt_id), and inspect the output. This would reflect the maximal model in that it includes all possible random slopes.

title: Mixed effects models
text:
5.3 Model selection
You might have noticed that R printed a warning during model fitting: boundary (singular) fit: see help(‘isSingular’). In the summary output, you can see that the intercepts and slopes for ppt_id are perfectly negatively correlated (-1.00). You can see this for yourself if you plot the random effects as we did above—when participants have high intercept values, they have smaller condition values.
We would not expect such perfectly correlated values, and the warning indicates that the model could not be estimated properly. In this situation, we would typically simplify the model (i.e., remove random effects components) until the warning goes away, though there isn’t a consensus on the best procedure. This is what we mean when we say the models can be challenging to fit!

title: Mixed effects models
text:
7.1 Challenge yourself
We fitted a linear mixed effects model on response time data, a continuous variable. Mixed effects models are extremely flexible, and we can also use them to model accuracy data (which have binary values of 0 and 1). The underlying maths is different, but the process of fitting them in R is largely the same.
Try to figure out how to analyse the accuracy data available in this dataset. You will need to find the function for running a binomial mixed effects model, and specify the family as you run it.
Can you fit a maximal random effects structure for this model?


Show solutions
# Fit logistic regression model on accuracy data
acc_mod <- glmer(acc ~ sleep + (1+sleep|ppt_id) + (1+sleep|item), 
                 family = "binomial", data = sleep_dat) 

# Inspect output
summary(acc_mod)
## Note that the coefficients are not directly interpretable in these models

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
The aim of this practical is to get used to the R environment. The best way to do this is to start with something you already know about: basic statistics from your first and second year. Along the way we will introduce basic concepts common to all programming languages, with no prior programming knowledge assumed.






Learning objectives



By the end of this practical, you will be able to:

Use RStudio to write, comment, and execute lines of code.
Create and manipulate objects in R.
Load data files into R.
Calculate basic summary statistics.
Implement common inferential tests, including a t-test, correlation, and ANOVA.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
2.1 Top left: Scripts
The top left quadrant is for your scripts. You won’t see this quadrant when you first open R, but it will appear when you create one in Section 3.
Scripts are like lists of instructions for the computer to follow. You can save them for future use, and this makes it easy to set up complex analyses without typing them in by hand each time or needing to click through multiple options.
Throughout these practicals, you will create several scripts that you can later adapt and reuse in running statistical analyses.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
2.2 Bottom left: Console
The lower left window is called the Console. This is where the magic happens! Here, you can type in individual commands to ask the computer to do something. You can use it just like a calculator: try clicking in the console and typing 20 + 57 (or any other sum you choose!). If you press the Enter/Return key, the answer will print below.
We can also instruct the computer to create an “object” (or “variable”1). An object is like a box that you can store information in. Some objects are big, such as large datasets that contain many numbers or even chunks of text. Others might contain only one number.
Let’s create an object called a, and give it the value 5. Click on the Console area and type:

a <- 5

Then hit the Enter/Return key to run it. You will encounter the arrows <- a lot in R: they are used to assign (or store) everything on the right to the name that you provide on the left2.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
2.3 Top right: Environment
If you have created an object, a, it should now appear in the top right section, in the Environment tab. This means that we can now treat a as though it is a number: we can run mathematical operations on the object, and get out an answer that depends on the value assigned. Try this now by typing a*2 into the console to multiply it by two, or a^2 to square it.
So why not just type 5^2 in the first place? Objects are useful because we can change and update their values, or include many numbers in them. Let’s make a new object called b with the numbers 1-5, and see what happens when we square it:

b <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
b^2

You should see that we now get a list of the squares of all the elements.
We will use objects to store and manipulate data in R, similar to how we might work on a spreadsheet or SPSS file. You can always inspect the objects you have to hand and the values assigned to them in the Environment panel.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
2.4 Bottom right: Other things!
The bottom right window has several sections that can be navigated by clicking on the tabs at the top. Files shows the files in the directory that we are working from, Plots will contain any figures that we create, Packages contains a list of extensions that will enable us to do different types of statistics, and the Help table will show the help pages for a particular function if we ask for them (we’ll do this a lot!).

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
3.1 Opening your R Project
Make sure that you are working in the R Project ARM_Practicals. This should be the case if you have just completed the set-up instructions instructions. If not, or if you closed RStudio in between, you can open this by clicking File >> Open Project… and navigating to the project file we created.
Remember, it should say “ARM_Practicals” in the top-right corner of the RStudio window.



Current R Project open

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
3.2 Creating a script
You can create a new script by clicking File >> New File >> R Script, or using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+N.
Now you have a script open, let’s save it so that we can retain our work beyond today. Click File >> Save As… and navigate to the scripts folder inside the ARM_Practicals folder you created. Once you are in this folder, save your script with the name ARM1_intro.R.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
3.3 Loading data into R
There is a file in the Practical Materials section of the VLE called ARM1_data1_gamers.csv. This is a .csv file, which is a readily used data storage format that can be opened in many different software3. Download this file, and save it in the folder we previously created (likely Documents/ARM_Practicals/data/).
At the top of your script file, you can now instruct R to read in the dataset by adding the following line:

gamer_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM1_data1_gamers.csv")

We are creating an object in R here called gamer_dat, and using the <- to assign something to it. Here, we want to assign the data file that we load in, so need to instruct it to find and load the data file. We use read.csv() to tell R that we want to load in a csv file. We tell it the file path to where the dataset is stored: the ./ affirms that we are starting in the current directory (your R project folder), then data/ instructs it to look in the data folder, then the final part is the name of the file (including the .csv extension).
Now you have typed this into your script, you need to execute it. You can do this by highlighting it with your mouse and then clicking ‘Run’ at the top of the script. Alternatively, if your cursor is on the correct line, you can hit Ctrl + Enter on your keyboard.
If you are successful, you should see an object called gamer_dat appear in the Environment tab. The information tells us it has 100 observations (rows) for 5 variables (columns). If you click the little grid to the right of this description, you can inspect the dataset in your top left panel. The five columns of the dataset correspond to:

ppt_id: a unique identifying code for each participant
age_years: their age in years
gamer: whether they play video games (y) or not (n)
hours: if they do play video games, how many hours they play per week on average (or NA if they don’t, meaning that it’s a missing value)
wmc: working memory capacity

This dataset was simulated for the purposes of today’s practical, but was inspired by a research study by Dr Fiona McNab.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
5.1 Running a t-test
In Years 1 and 2, you learned about some inferential statistics that test the relationship between two variables.
Let’s test the hypothesis that gamers versus non-gamers have different working memory capacity in our dataset. We can use a t-test to analyse the difference in means between two groups. Add the following line of code to your script:

t.test(wmc ~ gamer, data = gamer_dat)

Within the t.test() call, we have asked for our dependent variable (wmc) to be predicted by (~) the variable gamer, which we know has two levels in the dataset (y, n). We don’t actually have objects called wmc and gamer in our R environment, so we need to specify that it should look for these within the gamer_dat dataset.
Execute the line of code. The output should reiterate the test you have run, and provide the necessary values for reporting on the third line of output: the t-statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value.
Is there a significant difference between the two groups (p < .05)? What is the mean working memory capacity for each group?

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
5.2 Running a correlation
Another simple analysis for testing the relationship between two variables is a correlation: the strength of association between two continuous variables. Let’s test how working memory capacity relates to age by typing and executing the following line.

cor.test(formula = ~ age_years + wmc, data = gamer_dat)

Again, the output should tell you the test that has been done. Does the p-value show that there’s a significant relationship between the two? The final line of output (labelled “cor”) is the correlation coefficient. What happens to working memory as age increases?






Getting help with functions



These calls for statistical tests that we have just run are called functions. We also used functions above to read in the data, and gain some summary statistics. You can find out more about the options available for each function by typing e.g., help(t.test) or help(cor.test) in the Console (this is a bit meta, we use the help() function to ask for help about other functions). This should bring up some helpful information in the bottom right window.
The help pages tell you which “Arguments” you need to give to the function, and how to specify them. For example, we can see that to run a Spearman test rather than a Pearson’s correlation, we should add the argument method = "spearman" inside the brackets. Try this now.

title: Week 1: Introduction to R
text:
5.3 Running an ANOVA
Finally, let’s run a simple one-way ANOVA. Now you’ve established that gamers have a higher working memory capacity than non-gamers, we might want to ask whether it matters what type of games people are playing. You run a new study and recruit only young adults who self-report as gamers. You measure their working capacity, and ask them to select their dominant game type.
Make sure that you have downloaded the data from the VLE and saved it in your data folder. Load it into R and assign it to an object called type_dat. Inspect the dataset to see the game categories.

type_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM1_data2_gametype.csv")

Given there are three levels of game type, we can no longer use a t-test to compare working memory between groups. Instead, we can use a one-way ANOVA.
The first step in running an ANOVA is to check the assumption of homogeneity of variance using Levene’s test. This test isn’t included as standard in R, so we need to load in a package (a set of functions that someone has written) to run it. You only need to run this once in each R session. Add the following lines to your script5, and run them:

# Load car package
library(car)

# Run Levene's test
leveneTest(wmc ~ type, data = type_dat)

The output prints a warning message to say that that it interpreted our group (i.e., game type) as a factor. This is fine, that’s what we want it to do! You should then see that the test is not significant (p > .05), so we can assume that the variances are equal across the groups. This means we can proceed with our ANOVA.
We can run the test and display the results using only two lines of code:

# Run ANOVA and save output to object
gametype_model <- aov(wmc ~ type, data = type_dat)

# Print output summary
summary(gametype_model)

This will produce your ANOVA summary table as follows:


            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
type         2   40.3  20.144   4.806 0.0105 *
Residuals   87  364.7   4.192                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Just like in SPSS, we can pick out the degrees of freedom (2, 87), the F ratio (4.81) and the p-value (.01). This tells us that there is a significant difference in working memory capacity depending on the type of game that people play most regularly.

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
The aim of this week’s practical is to walk through some key steps involved in conducting a meta-analysis. We will use a recently published meta-analysis that examined the relationship between procedural learning and reading ability.
The Procedural Deficit Hypothesis proposes that reading and language disorders stem from a difficulty in the procedural learning system—i.e., the system that underpins the learning of probabilistic knowledge (Ullman et al., 2020). Procedural learning is often measured using Serial Reaction Time (SRT) tasks: participants respond to a repeating sequence of stimuli (e.g., different button presses), and their improvements in speed over several blocks are measured as an index of learning. However, evidence that SRT performance is associated with reading ability is mixed, with some studies showing a strong association and others finding nothing at all. Many studies in this area suffer from small sample sizes, making it hard to draw sound conclusions.
A meta-analysis provides a valuable way of summarising this evidence. This meta-analysis was conducted by a former PhD student at York, Dr Catia Oliveira, together with Professor Lisa Henderson and Dr Emma Hayiou-Thomas. We will use part of their dataset to showcase the different steps in conducting a meta-analysis.






Learning objectives



As a reminder, this week’s learning objectives are to:

Explain the purpose and value of meta-analytic approaches
Describe key stages of conducting a meta-analysis
Compare different approaches to weighting and pooling effect sizes
Interpret the results of a meta-analysis
Assess the impact of publication bias on meta-analytic findings

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
2.1 Extract effect sizes
In this week’s practical section on the VLE, you should find a file named ARM2_data_srt_gaps.csv. Download this file and save it in the ARM_Practicals/data/ folder you created last week.






Tip



If you don’t have this folder on your current machine, repeat the set-up steps from Week 1.


Open this file in Excel to start with. This is a stripped back version of the published meta-analysis. You can see that we have the following columns:

Study: the authors and year of publication
N: the sample size
Age: the average age of the sample
Task: the reading task administered
Group: whether the participants had developmental dyslexia (DD) or not (TD)
Cor: the correlation coefficient, r

You will see that a few cells are blank. We need to extract this information from the relevant papers before we begin! Inspect the following papers to fill in the missing sample sizes and correlation coefficients:

Clark & Lum (2017). (Hint: Inspect Table 3. You want to know the correlation between the procedural learning (SRTT) and nonword (phonemic decoding efficiency) tasks.)
Schmalz et al. (2021). (Hint: Inspect Table 2. The correlations in the meta-analysis reflect each of the word reading and pseudoword reading measures with the SRTT difference)

Make sure you check carefully that all cells of the table are filled before proceeding. Then save your new version of the file as ARM2_data_srt_complete.csv in the same data folder.

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
2.2 Setting up in RStudio
Now that we have extracted information from our identified studies, let’s get set up in R. In your ARM_Practicals folder, double click the ARM_Practicals.Rproj file to open it in RStudio.
Create a new R script (using the button at the top-left of your window), and save it as ARM2_meta-analysis.R in your scripts folder.
Start by loading the necessary packages for today’s exercises. You will need to first install the metafor package for meta-analysis by running install.packages("metafor"). You should only need to run this once on any device, so you don’t need to add this to your script. We will also be using the tidyverse package for some basic data manipulation tasks. This is already installed on university machines, but you might need to install it in the same way if you are working on a personal device.
Once you’ve installed the packages, add the following lines to the top of your script and run them to load the packages.

# Load packages
library(tidyverse) # for data cleaning
library(metafor)   # for meta-analysis

The next step is to load the data. If you have opened your R project and have saved the data in the data folder, you should be able to read it in as follows.

# Read in extracted effect sizes and study info
full_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM2_data_srt_complete.csv")

The dataset includes studies of people with dyslexia as well as those without reading difficulties. Let’s start by focusing just on those individuals without reading difficulties. We can do this using the filter() function from the tidyverse package that we loaded above. We tell R to filter (or subset) the dataset to keep the rows where the Group column is listed as “TD”, and store the result as td_dat.

td_dat <- filter(full_dat, Group == "TD")

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
2.3 Compute sampling variance
The dataset includes a correlation coefficient for each study, which is our effect size for this meta-analysis. It quantifies the direction and strength of relationship between SRT task performance and reading ability. However, some of the studies have much larger sample sizes than others. Use min(td_dat$N) to identify the smallest sample size in the dataset, and then use the max() function to identify the largest.
To capture this uncertainty around the correlation estimates, we should compute their variance ahead of running the meta-analysis. Our meta-analysis package provides a handy function for doing this:

td_dat_var <- escalc(measure = "COR",   # specify effect size measure
                     ri = Cor,          # specify correlation variable
                     ni = N,            # specify sample size variable
                     data = td_dat)     # dataset

If you look to your Environment window (top right), you should now see an object called td_dat_var. If you click the grid to open it, you should find two extra columns at the end:

yi: your effect size, which in this case is identical to the one in the Cor column as we haven’t asked it to do any kind of transformation
vi: your sampling variances, which have now been calculated based on the correlation coefficient and sample size

Now we’re ready to run the analysis!

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
3.1 Fixed effects meta-analysis
In a fixed effects analysis, we assume that all studies are measuring the same underlying true effect size, and calculate the average effect size across the included studies. Use the rma() function to run this as follows:

# Fixed effects model
fixed_mod <- rma(yi = yi, vi = vi,
                 method = "FE", data = td_dat_var)

We’ve specified the variables with our effect size estimates and sampling variance (already conveniently named the same by the escalc() function above). We’ve then specified the “FE” method for fixed effects, and the dataset to use.
Use the summary() function on the model object to inspect the results.
The output tells us that we ran a Fixed-Effects model with 73 effect sizes. The pooled estimate for the correlation coefficient is ~0.04, showing a very small yet statistically significant correlation.

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
3.2 Random effects meta-analysis
The random effects model assumes that the samples in the meta-analysis are a random sample from a larger population of studies that could plausibly have been/will be conducted. We can fit this alternative model simply by changing the method argument within the meta-analysis function. The package provides several different ways to estimate the heterogeneity between studies (you can see these listed in the documentation by running help(rma)), but for now we will stick with the default option.

# Random effects model
random_mod <- rma(yi = yi, vi = vi,
                 method = "REML", data = td_dat_var)
summary(random_mod)

You should see from the results that the coefficient estimate has shrunk slightly and is no longer significant. These are both valid models but have different inferences: the fixed effects model tells us that there is a very small but significant correlation across the available datasets, but when we consider heterogeneity between effect sizes in the random effects model, we see that this effect size is likely even smaller in the wider population.

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
section: 4.1 Under the hood: computing inverse variance
text:
4.1 Under the hood: computing inverse variance
One of the most common ways to do this is via inverse-variance, which the rma() function does by default. If you inspect your td_dat_var data frame, you will see that the smaller samples have the highest variance (vi). You can click on the column header to order the data by this variable, so that you can see this for yourself.
To use this variance in the analysis, the model uses the inverse (1/variance), so that smaller samples have the smallest weighting. The function does this under the hood, but you can see what this looks like by calculating it for yourself:

td_dat_inv <- mutate(td_dat_var, inv_var = 1/vi)

Here we used the mutate() function (from the tidyverse package) to make a change to the existing dataframe td_dat_var. We provide the name of the new variable, inv_var, and specify that this variable should be computed as 1 divided by the variance variable vi. We assigned the new version of the dataset to a new object, td_dat_inv.
Inspect this new object by clicking the grid icon in your Environment window. You should now see that your inv_var column has larger numbers for studies with larger sample sizes (N).

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
4.2 Changing weights in the meta-analysis
Because weighting by inverse variance is a very common and sensible approach, the rma() meta-analysis function does this by default. This means you’ve already weighted your samples in your above models!
To compare, try fitting two new models (fixed, random) and include the argument weighted = FALSE. Use a different object name to store the model output, so that you can inspect the differences in output when you call summary().
Alternatively, you can try weighting by sample size alone, by setting weights = N.

title: Week 2: Meta-analysis
text:
7.1 Challenge yourself
Often we are interested in how effect sizes vary across different conditions. In this case, the researchers were interested in whether the relationship between procedural learning (SRT) and reading ability might differ depending on the participant groups tested.
If you finish the practical in good time or want to push your skills further beyond the end of today’s session, see if you can test whether participant Group is a moderator in your analysis. Use the original data file that you loaded in (full_dat), which also includes effect sizes for samples with developmental dyslexia. You can look at the help files or use Google to find out how to include this extra predictor.


Show solutions
## Compute sampling variance for full dataset
full_dat_var <- escalc(measure = "COR",  # specify effect size measure
                       ri = Cor,         # specify correlation variable
                       ni = N,           # specify sample size variable
                       data = full_dat)  # dataset

## Run model with Group factor as moderator
group_mod <- rma(yi = yi, vi = vi, mods = ~ factor(Group),
                 method = "REML", data = full_dat_var)
summary(group_mod)  # no effect of group (p = 0.159)

title: Quantile Regression
text:
This week we’ve learned about a semi-parametric alternative to linear regression that does not assume normally distributed errors. We’ve also seen how the quantile approach can be extended to ask more nuanced questions about the data: moving beyond “Does X have a relationship with Y?” to “How does the relationship between X and Y vary?”.
In this session, we’ll put this into practice using an educational dataset on reading abilities. It is well-established that successful reading depends on both reading accuracy and language comprehension. While reading accuracy is a major constraint for beginning readers, we expect it to account for less variance in more skilled readers once those skills are fluent. In turn, variability in language skills might come to account for more of the variability in reading success.
We will use data from Year 8 pupils (age 12-13 years) to look at how these two variables—reading accuracy and language (vocabulary)—predict reading comprehension across the spectrum of reading ability. These data were collected as part of a larger project on reading comprehension (James et al., 2021).






Learning objectives



As a reminder, this week’s learning objectives are to:

Explain the key assumptions and limitations of linear regression
Explain when and why quantile regression might be preferred
Describe and interpret quantile regression as a method for modelling the conditional median of an outcome
Explain how quantile regression uses weighted errors to model other parts of the outcome distribution
Compare and interpret regression coefficients across quantiles to understand how associations vary across the outcome distribution

title: Quantile Regression
text:
2.1 Create a script
Start with the usual set-up steps for the practical sessions:

Open your ARM_Practicals.Rproj file in RStudio
Create a new script and save it in your scripts/ folder as ARM4_quantile.R
Download the data for the Week 4 practical from the VLE, and save it in your data/ folder.







Tip

title: Quantile Regression
text:
2.2 Load packages
We will need the quantreg package today’s session, which you will first need to install using either the packages tab or by running install.packages("quantreg") in the Console.
Once you have done this, load the package at the top of your new script:

library(quantreg)

title: Quantile Regression
text:
2.3 Load data
Now read in the data from your data/ folder.

read_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM4_data_reading.csv")

The dataset consists of the following variables:

ppt_id: a unique identifier for each participant
read_comp: score on the reading comprehension test
read_acc: composite score from the reading accuracy tests (Z-score)
vocab: score on the vocabulary test (Z-score)

Our reading accuracy variable was Z-scored so that we could calculate a mean score across different tests (whereas averaging the original test scores would not have worked when the tests were on different scales). Z-scores produce a standardised score with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. We did the same to the vocabulary measure so that our predictors will be on the same scale.
Remember that you can inspect the data by clicking the grid icon in the Environment window. Try calculating the mean and standard deviation of the different variables, as we did in Week 1.


Show the code
# Reading comprehension (outcome measure)
mean(read_dat$read_comp)
sd(read_dat$read_comp)

# Reading accuracy (Z-scored predictor)
mean(read_dat$read_acc)
sd(read_dat$read_acc)

# Vocabulary (Z-scored predictor)
mean(read_dat$vocab)
sd(read_dat$vocab)

title: Quantile Regression
text:
7.1 Challenge yourself
I have written some code to plot the relationship between reading accuracy and reading comprehension on a scatterplot, using a popular data visualisation package ggplot2. I have extracted and plotted the ordinary least squares regression line from our first model (read_lm) and then the median regression line from our quantile model (read_rq, tau = 0.5).
Start by copying and running this code.

# Load package for data visualisation
library(ggplot2)

# Specify dataframe and x/y variables 
ggplot(read_dat, aes(x = read_acc, y = read_comp)) + 
  
  # Add individual data points from dataset
  geom_point(shape = 1) + 
  
  # Use theme for transparent background 
  theme_classic() + 
  
  # Add regression line from standard linear model
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_lm)[["(Intercept)"]], 
              slope = coef(read_lm)[["read_acc"]],
              linetype = "longdash", size = 1) + 
  
  # Add regression line from quantile model, tau = 0.5 (median)
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_rq)[["(Intercept)", "tau= 0.5"]],
              slope = coef(read_rq)[["read_acc", "tau= 0.5"]], 
              colour = "blue", size = 1) 

Now copy the section for plotting the median regression line twice more, and edit it to add the regression lines for tau = 0.1 and 0.9. You will need to add a + sign between each section so that the code continues to add each element to the plot. Try editing the colour or linetype to distinguish between your lines.


Show solutions
# Specify dataframe and x/y variables 
ggplot(read_dat, aes(x = read_acc, y = read_comp)) + 
  
  # Add individual data points from dataset
  geom_point(shape = 1) + 
  
  # Use theme for transparent background 
  theme_classic() + 
  
  # Add regression line from standard linear model
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_lm)[["(Intercept)"]], 
              slope = coef(read_lm)[["read_acc"]],
              linetype = "longdash", size = 1) + 
  
  # Add regression line from quantile model, tau = 0.5 (median)
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_rq)[["(Intercept)", "tau= 0.5"]],
              slope = coef(read_rq)[["read_acc", "tau= 0.5"]], 
              colour = "blue", size = 1) + 
  
  # Add regression line from quantile model, tau = 0.1 (median)
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_rq)[["(Intercept)", "tau= 0.1"]],
              slope = coef(read_rq)[["read_acc", "tau= 0.1"]], 
              colour = "red", size = 1) +
  
  # Add regression line from quantile model, tau = 0.5 (median)
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(read_rq)[["(Intercept)", "tau= 0.9"]],
              slope = coef(read_rq)[["read_acc", "tau= 0.9"]], 
              colour = "green", size = 1) 


Once you’re done, you could also copy and edit the code to plot the relationship between vocabulary and reading comprehension.
If you’re interested in learning more about data visualisation in R, you might want to spend some time figuring out what each element contributes to the plot (there’s also a whole DataCamp course you can try!).

text:
2.1 Preparation
We expect that you will come to this session having attended the lecture on Tuesday, or caught up via the recording if you were unable to make it in person. We also recommend that you should have done the core reading for the week to consolidate your understanding. Having done so will help you to engage fully with the practical session, and also enable you to ask questions about aspects that you did not understand.

title: 1 Introduction to the module
text:
2.2 During the practical
The practical is self-paced. You should work through the instructions to create and annotate your own analysis script, checking your understanding and taking notes as you go.
Where we have hidden code sections, do your best to try and figure out the solution yourself before peeking! Trial and error is a much more effective way of learning, and will help you to build your coding skills.
You can count on getting stuck at various points during the practical sessions. Errors are a very normal part of coding, even if sometimes frustrating! If you get stuck, try the following:

Spend time trying some different things! What’s happening that you don’t expect? Is there an error message, and does it tell you anything useful?
Google it! Copying and pasting the error message into Google often takes you to help forums where others have asked about the same problem.
Chat to the person next to you—maybe they can spot something in your code that you can’t see?
Put your hand up, and we’ll come over to help!
